The '''Content Authenticity Initiative''' ('''CAI''') is an industry [[Advocacy group|advocacy coalition]]<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.siia.net/articles/standards-for-trust-blog-recap |title=Standards for Trust: How industry and government are working to combat deepfakes and inauthentic content |last=Joseph |first=Jeff |publisher=Software and Information Industry Association |date=2020-11-20 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201202222701/https://www.siia.net/articles/standards-for-trust-blog-recap |archive-date=2020-12-02 |access-date=2026-09-13}}</ref> and corporate business unit of [[Adobe Inc.]] that promotes the adoption of digital media provenance and attribution standards. Founded to mitigate digital misinformation,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Robertson |first=Adi |date=2019-11-04 |title=Adobe and Twitter are designing a system for permanently attaching artists' names to pictures |url=https://www.theverge.com/2019/11/4/20948229/adobe-twitter-nyt-company-content-authenticity-initiative-attribution-misinformation-tool |access-date=2022-06-30 |website=The Verge |language=en}}</ref> the organization advocates for an open, interoperable framework to establish verifiable transparency for [[Digital asset|digital assets.]]

The initiative engages in public education,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://edex.adobe.com/cai |title=Teach media literacy with the Content Authenticity Initiative |publisher=Adobe Education Exchange|date=2023-05-18 |access-date=2026-07-12}}</ref> industry outreach,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.wired.com/sponsored/story/content-authenticitys-chain-of-trust-reaches-cameras/ |title=Content Authenticity's Chain of Trust Reaches Cameras |magazine=Wired |date=2022-10-27 |type=Sponsored content via WIRED Brand Lab|access-date=2026-07-12}}</ref> and regulatory advocacy<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.schumer.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Andy%20Parsons%20-%20Statement.pdf |title=Statement of Andy Parsons, Senior Director, Content Authenticity Initiative, Adobe |date=2023-11-08 |access-date=2026-07-12}}</ref> regarding [[digital safety]] and [[artificial intelligence (AI)]] transparency standardizations. Structurally, the CAI supports the deployment of specifications developed by two technical standards organizations: the [[#Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity | Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA)]] and the [[#Creators Assertions Working Group |Creators Assertions Working Group (CAWG)]]. To facilitate ecosystem adoption, the CAI develops and maintains [[#Open-source software| open-source software development kits (SDKs)]] that allow software engineers to integrate provenance tracking features directly into third-party applications and digital services.

The primary consumer-facing implementation of this technical architecture is branded as [[Content Credentials]]. Content Credentials function as tamper-evident [[metadata]] packages cryptographically bound to digital media files. These packages record structural provenance, asset attribution, and historical editing data over the lifecycle of a digital file.

== Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity ==

The '''Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity''' ('''C2PA''') is an open, cross-industry technical standards body established on February 22, 2021.<ref>{{cite web |last=Ross |first=Craig |date=2021-02-22 |title=C2PA Founding Press Release |url=https://c2pa.org/c2pa-founding-press-release/ |publisher=Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) |access-date=2026-09-23}}</ref>
It was formed to unify the technical specifications of two existing content attribution frameworks: the Adobe-led Content Authenticity Initiative (CAI) and Project Origin, a joint news-ecosystem initiative created by Microsoft<ref>{{cite web |title=Project Origin: Building trust at the origin |url=https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/project/project-origin/ |publisher=Microsoft Research |access-date=2026-09-23}}</ref> and the BBC.<ref>{{cite web |last=Ellis |first=Laura |date=2021-03-15 |title=Project Origin: one year on |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/mediacentre/articles/2021/project-origin-one-year-on |publisher=BBC Media Centre |access-date=2026-09-23}}</ref>
The six founding corporate members of the coalition were Adobe, Arm, BBC, Intel, Microsoft, and Truepic. The C2PA operates structurally as a project under the Joint Development Foundation (JDF), an affiliate of the [[Linux Foundation]].

=== Governance and Leadership ===
Upon its formation in 2021, the organization's governance structure separated administrative, technical, and public policy leadership:

* '''Chair''': Andrew Jenks, Director of Content Integrity at [[Microsoft]], served as the overall Chair of the organization.<ref>{{cite web |title=C2PA Releases Draft Spec |url=https://contentcredentials.org/c2pa-releases-draft-spec/ |publisher=Content Credentials |date=2021-09-01 |access-date=2026-09-23}}</ref>

* '''Technical Working Group Chair''': Leonard Rosenthol, Senior Principal Scientist at [[Adobe Inc.|Adobe]], was appointed to oversee the development of technical specification drafts.<ref>{{cite web |last=Rosenthol |first=Leonard |date=2021-10-01 |title=Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) for Media Extensions Interest Group |url=https://www.w3.org/2011/webtv/wiki/images/5/5c/C2PA_for_MEIG-opt.pdf |format=PDF |publisher=W3C Media Extensions Interest Group |access-date=2026-09-23}}</ref>

* '''Government Affairs Committee Co-Chairs''': Mounir Ibrahim, Chief Communications Officer and Head of Public Affairs at [[Hany_Farid#Truepic|Truepic]] (formerly with the [[U.S. Department of State]]), and Matt Schrader, Director of Government Relations and Public Policy at [[Adobe Inc.|Adobe]] (formerly Vice President at [[Dutko Worldwide]]), were appointed to lead the organization's public policy and government relations efforts.

In 2026, Clément Wolf, Director of Responsible AI Strategy, Trust & Safety at [[Google]], succeeded Andrew Jenks as the overall Chair of the C2PA.<ref>{{cite web |date=2026-07-28 |title=C2PA Welcomes TikTok to Steering Committee, Advancing the Adoption of Content Credentials at a Global Scale |url=https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/c2pa-welcomes-tiktok-to-steering-committee-advancing-the-adoption-of-content-credentials-at-a-global-scale-302836730.html |publisher=PR Newswire |access-date=2026-09-23}}</ref>

=== Organizational support ===
While the C2PA operates as an independent technical standards body, it receives operational and external engagement support directly from its member corporations.<ref>{{cite web |title=Public Comment on NIST Executive Order 14110 Tasks (NIST-2023-0009-0036) |url=https://www.regulations.gov/comment/NIST-2023-0009-0036 |publisher=Regulations.gov |date=2023-12-01 |access-date=2026-09-23}}</ref>
According to corporate accountability reports submitted to European Union regulators, Adobe dedicates internal employees from its Communications and Public Policy divisions to manage global outreach, press relations, and regulatory advocacy for the C2PA framework.<ref>{{cite web |title=Adobe Report March 2025 |url=https://disinfocode.eu/reports/adobe/5?commitmentId=220&chapterId=44 |publisher=EU Code of Practice on Disinformation Transparency Centre |date=2025-03-01 |access-date=2026-09-23}}</ref>

The coalition also partners The [[Information Technology Industry Council]] (ITI) and The  [[Information Technology and Innovation Foundation]] (ITIF) to promote its provenance specifications.<ref>{{cite web |date=2026-03-05 |title=Context Matters: Building Trust in Digital Content |url=https://itif.org/events/2026/03/05/context-matters-building-trust-in-digital-content/ |website=Information Technology and Innovation Foundation |access-date=2026-10-16}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=2026-02-20 |title=ITI Convenes Global Government and Tech Leaders at 2026 India AI Impact Summit |url=https://www.itic.org/news-events/news-releases/iti-convenes-global-government-and-tech-leaders-at-2026-india-ai-impact-summit |website=Information Technology Industry Council |access-date=2026-10-16}}</ref>

== Creators Assertions Working Group ==
The '''Creators Assertions Working Group''' ('''CAWG''') is a standards development organization that defines supplementary standards for digital identity, publishing, licensing, and schema-based assertions.<ref >{{cite web |last=Perry |first=Scott |title=How can I trust online information? |url=https://cawg.io/about/trust-online-information/ |publisher=Creator Assertions Working Group (CAWG) |access-date=2026-09-23}}</ref>
These specifications function as extensions to the Content Credentials framework established by the C2PA. The primary purpose of the CAWG specifications is to allow content creators to securely bind a digital identity to digital content, establishing authorship within the C2PA ecosystem.

Initial technical development on the Identity "2.0" assertion model began in September 2023<ref>{{cite web |last=Howland |first=Char |date=2023-10-04 |title=2023-09-21: Identity Special Interest Group |url=https://lf-hyperledger.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/IWG/pages/18252178/2023-09-21+Identity+Special+Interest+Group |access-date=2026-09-26 |website=LF Decentralized Trust}}</ref> under Adobe's Eric Scouten, who managed early private drafts and presented the framework to the Internet Identity Workshop and the Content Authenticity Initiative (CAI) Summit.<ref>{{cite web |last=Scouten |first=Eric |date=2024-02-21 |title=C2PA and Identity: Technical overview for Trust Over IP Foundation |url=https://northernblock.io/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/2024-02-20-ToIP-C2PA-and-identity-overview.pdf |format=PDF |access-date=2026-09-23}}</ref>
The CAWG formally originated as an Adobe-led working group in early 2024 to host the identity specification alongside other custom assertions removed from the core C2PA 2.0 standard (including training, data mining, and endorsements). In March 2025, the CAWG joined the Decentralized Identity Foundation (DIF) to operate as an independent standards group under a joint collaboration agreement with the Trust Over IP Project and the [[Linux Foundation]] Decentralized Trust.<ref>{{cite web |title=Welcoming Creator Assertions Working Group to DIF |date=2025-03-03 |url=https://blog.identity.foundation/welcome-cawg/ |publisher=Decentralized Identity Foundation (DIF) |access-date=2026-09-23}}</ref>

== Open-source software ==
The CAI manages a suite of [[open-source]] software reference implementations for the C2PA and the CAWG specifications.<ref>{{Cite web |title=CAI open source SDK |url=https://opensource.contentauthenticity.org |access-date=2026-07-15 |language=en}}</ref> While the projects are branded under the CAI umbrella, software development and repository maintenance are driven almost entirely by [[Adobe Inc.|Adobe]] under a corporate-led, single-vendor governance model.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Adobe contributor license agreement |url=https://github.com/contentauth/c2pa-rs/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#contributor-license-agreement |access-date=2026-07-15 |language=en}}</ref>

Within the documentation, the [[Proprietary software|proprietary]] '''Adobe Content Authenticity Inspect''' (ACA Inspect) application is promoted as a ''C2PA conforming validator'' for [[Content Credentials]].<ref>{{cite web |author=Content Authenticity Initiative |title=Using the inspect tool on Adobe Content Authenticity (Beta) |url=https://opensource.contentauthenticity.org/docs/getting-started/inspect |website=CAI Open Source Documentation |date=2026-01-01 |access-date=2026-10-11}}</ref> Independent technology researchers and critics have noted a divergence between the software's implementation and the initiative's stated objectives. While the broader CAI ecosystem emphasizes open-source development and outlines user privacy as a core guiding principle, the consumer-facing "Inspect" application remains proprietary and utilizes analytics and identification cookies.<ref>{{cite web |last=Krawetz |first=Neal |title=C2PA and the All Adobe Show |url=https://www.hackerfactor.com/blog/index.php?/archives/1048-C2PA-and-the-All-Adobe-Show.html |website=The Hacker Factor Blog |date=2024-10-31 |access-date=2026-10-11}}</ref>

=== C2PA tool ===
The C2PA Tool<ref>{{Cite web |title=Command line tool for displaying and adding C2PA manifests |url=https://github.com/contentauth/c2patool |access-date=2026-09-25 |language=en}}</ref> is the official [[command-line interface]] utility developed to read, cryptographically sign, and verify [[Content Credentials]] directly within [[digital media]] assets.

=== C2PA Verify/C2PA Conformance Tool ===
The C2PA Conformance Tool<ref>{{cite web |url=https://c2pa-conformulator.netlify.app/ |title=C2PA Conformance Tool |website=[[Netlify]] |publisher=Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) |access-date=2026-09-27}}</ref> is a web application used to validate C2PA manifests and CAWG assertions associated with media files. The tool evaluates digital assets against a set of rules written in [[YAML]] to make sure they follow the official guidelines.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://github.com/contentauth/c2pa-conformance-tool |title=contentauth/c2pa-conformance-tool: A web application for validating C2PA manifests in media files |author=Content Authenticity Initiative |website=[[GitHub]] |date=2026-02-18 |access-date=2026-09-27}}</ref>

=== Software development kits and libraries ===
The ecosystem is built around a core [[Rust (programming language) |Rust]] library. <ref>{{Cite web |title=CAI Rust library |url=https://github.com/contentauth/c2pa-rs |access-date=2026-09-25 |language=en}}</ref> Specialized language bindings and platform wrappers are maintained across several environments:
* System & Desktop: [[Rust (programming language) |Rust]], [[C++]], and [[Python (programming language)|Python]]
* Mobile Platforms: [[Android (operating system)|Android]] and [[iOS]]
* Web & JavaScript Runtimes: Web browsers via [[WebAssembly]] bindings, and [[Node.js]] via a compiled native binary addon.

== Provenance of information ==
{{More citations needed section|date=July 2026}}

[[File:Visual_glossary_of_C2PA_metadata.png|alt=Graphical representation of C2PA metadata structures|thumb|The structure of C2PA metadata in a file with multiple Manifests generated when the picture was recorded, edited and published]]

The procedures proposed by CAI and C2PA aim to address the widespread occurrence of disinformation<ref>{{Cite web |title=Measuring the reach of "fake news" and online disinformation in Europe |url=https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/our-research/measuring-reach-fake-news-and-online-disinformation-europe |access-date=2022-08-16 |website=Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Four key ways disinformation is spread online |url=https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2022/08/four-ways-disinformation-campaigns-are-propagated-online/ |access-date=2022-08-16 |website=World Economic Forum |language=en}}</ref> with a set of additional data (metadata) containing details about the provenance of information displayed on a digital device. Such information can be, for example, a photo, video, sound or [[text file]]. The C2PA metadata for this information can include, among other things, the publisher of the information, the device used to record the information, the location and time of the recording or editing steps that altered the information. To mitigate risks that the C2PA metadata might be changed unnoticed, it is secured with [[Cryptographic hash function|hashcodes]] and [[Public key certificate|certified]] [[Digital signature|digital signatures]]. The same applies to the main information content, such as a picture or a text. A hash code of that data is stored in the C2PA metadata section and then, as part of that metadata, secured with the digital signature.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Kennedy |first=Eamonn |date=2024-10-30 |title=C2PA – The digital sticker Big Tech is backing to battle our deep fake dilemma |url=https://storyful.com/c2pa-the-digital-sticker-big-tech-is-backing-to-battle-our-deep-fake-dilemma/ |access-date=2025-04-24 |website=Storyful |language=en-US}}</ref>

Securing metadata and the main content with certified signatures helps users to identify the provenance of a file they are currently viewing. If the C2PA metadata names, for example, a certain TV station as the publisher of a file, it is supposed to be very unlikely that the file originated from another source.

Files with C2PA-compliant metadata that are copied from a publisher's website and then published unaltered on social media (or elsewhere) still retain the provenance information. Users seeing that content on social media can examine such a file with an online tool offered by the CAI<ref>{{Cite web |title=Verify |url=https://verify.contentauthenticity.org/inspect |access-date=2022-08-16 |website=verify.contentauthenticity.org}}</ref> or, if present, with C2PA-compliant inspection tools of their own or those offered by the social media site. Standard-compliant tools are designed to detect whether there were any unauthorized modifications to the file or the metadata.

The methods proposed by CAI and C2PA do not allow for statements whether a content is "true", i.e., contains authentic information that faithfully reflects reality. Instead, C2PA-compliant metadata only offers reliable information about the origin of a piece of information. Whether users want to trust this information depends solely on their trust in its sources and the C2PA approach.

== Criticism ==
One criticism of C2PA is that it can compromise the privacy of people who sign things with it, due to the large amount of metadata in the digital labels it creates.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kaye |first=Kate|last2=Dixon |first2=Pam |date=2025-09-03 |title=Privacy in C2PA |url=https://worldprivacyforum.org/posts/privacy-identity-and-trust-in-c2pa/#_idTextAnchor027 |access-date=2026-08-01 |website=World Privacy Forum}}</ref>

Experts have also documented ways in which attackers can bypass C2PA’s safeguards, by altering provenance metadata, removing or forging watermarks, and mimicking digital fingerprints.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Krawetz |first=Neal |date=2024-05-09 |title=C2PA from the Attacker's Perspective - The Hacker Factor Blog |url=https://www.hackerfactor.com/blog/index.php?/archives/1031-C2PA-from-the-Attackers-Perspective.html |access-date=2025-04-24 |website=Hacker Factor}}</ref>

Besides the fact that C2PA doesn't address the question of whether the content is accurate, another shortcoming is that typical signing tools don't verify the accuracy of the metadata either, so users can't rely on the provenance data either unless they have reason to trust that the signer properly verified it.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Goals and Non-goals |url=https://spec.c2pa.org/specifications/specifications/2.4/explainer/Explainer.html#_goals_and_non_goals |access-date=2026-08-01 |website=C2PA Specifications |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Authenticated Contradictions from Desynchronized Provenance and Watermarking |url=https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.02378 |access-date=2026-08-01 |website=arXiv |language=en}}</ref>

== Members ==
As of September 2026, the CAI reports a total membership exceeding 5,000 participants, representing diverse organizations (non-profit, industry, media, education, government) as well as individuals.<ref >{{cite web |title=Our Members |url=https://contentauthenticity.org/our-members |publisher=Content Authenticity Initiative |access-date=2026-07-15}}</ref>

The official public member directory lists 1,053 entities,<ref >{{cite web |title=Member directory |url=https://contentauthenticity.org/our-members/directory |publisher=Content Authenticity Initiative |access-date=2026-09-25}}</ref> limited to formal institutional organizations, corporate partners, and members who have explicitly opted to establish a public profile.
